lessons.reflect: Think of a time you kept going with a failing approach well past when you should have stopped. What kept you committed?

lessons.title: Overestimating How Smoothly Others Will Cooperate
objectives: Recognise the planning fallacy as it applies to other people's cooperation, and plan for realistic friction instead.
teach: The planning fallacy is underestimating how long things take or how smoothly they'll go. Applied to other people specifically, it means assuming they'll cooperate, respond, or deliver on the timeline and terms you're hoping for, with less friction or disagreement than is realistic.

Planning around the best-case version of someone else's cooperation, rather than a realistic one based on how similar cooperation has actually gone before — with this person, or with people in similar roles generally.

This isn't cynicism about other people — it's the same correction the planning fallacy always calls for: look at how similar situations have actually gone in the past, rather than imagining this one will go unusually smoothly.
lessons.example: A project lead assumes three other departments will sign off on a shared proposal within a week, because that's the timeline that would be convenient. Looking at how long similar sign-offs have actually taken in the past — usually three weeks, with at least one round of pushback — gives a much more realistic plan than hoping this time will be different.
practicePrompts: Think of a plan that depends on someone else cooperating or delivering.
Ask how similar cooperation has actually gone in the past, not how you're hoping it goes.
Adjust your plan toward the realistic timeline, not the hopeful one.
lessons.apply: Before your next plan that depends on someone else's cooperation, look at how similar situations have actually gone before, and plan around that instead of the best case.
lessons.reflect: Think of a plan that fell apart because you assumed smoother cooperation from others than actually happened. What would looking at past patterns have told you?

lessons.title: Crediting Skill, Blaming Luck
objectives: Recognise self-serving attribution — crediting wins to skill and losses to luck — and weigh both consistently.
teach: Self-serving attribution is crediting your own skill and good decisions for a win, while blaming bad luck, an unfair opponent, or circumstances beyond your control for a loss — even when the actual causes were similar in both cases.

Not noticing the asymmetry itself. It feels natural in the moment, which is exactly what makes it easy to miss — the explanations offered for a win and a loss aren't being weighed by the same standard.

A useful check: would you accept the same kind of explanation from an opponent explaining their own win over you? If their 'I got lucky' wouldn't satisfy you as the full story, your own 'I got unlucky' probably isn't either.
lessons.example: After winning a negotiation, someone credits their sharp preparation and tactics. After losing a very similar negotiation the following month, the same person blames an unreasonable counterpart and bad timing — without considering that preparation, tactics, or luck may have played a similar role in both outcomes.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent win and a recent loss in a similar kind of situation.
Compare how you explained each one — skill for the win, luck or unfairness for the loss?
Consider applying the same standard of explanation to both.
lessons.apply: Next time you explain a win or a loss, apply the same standard to both — ask what role skill and luck each actually played, not just whichever story feels better.
lessons.reflect: Think of a loss you blamed mostly on bad luck or unfairness. Looking back honestly, how much of it was actually about your own decisions?

lessons.title: Mistaking Influence You Don't Have
objectives: Recognise the illusion of control and distinguish what you can actually influence in a situation from what you can't.
teach: The illusion of control is overestimating how much you can actually influence an outcome that depends heavily on chance, or on another player's independent choice you have no real way to affect.

Treating active involvement — effort, attention, ritual — as if it were the same thing as actual influence over the result. Doing more doesn't always mean controlling more, especially where the outcome genuinely depends on something outside your control.

The useful question isn't 'am I doing everything I can' — it's 'does what I'm doing actually change the probability of the outcome, or does it just feel like it does'. The two can come apart more than it feels like they would.
lessons.example: An investor checks stock prices multiple times a day, feeling that close attention gives her more control over the outcome. The checking itself changes nothing about where the price actually goes — it feels like involvement, but it isn't influence over a market driven by countless other independent decisions.
practicePrompts: Think of a situation where you feel like you have real influence over the outcome.
Ask honestly whether your actions actually change the probability of that outcome, or just feel like they do.
Consider what, if anything, you'd do differently if you accepted the real level of influence you have.
lessons.apply: Next time you notice yourself putting in extra effort toward an outcome, ask honestly whether that effort actually changes the odds, or just makes you feel more in control.
lessons.reflect: Think of a situation where you believed you had more influence than you actually did. What would recognising that earlier have changed?

lessons.title: The Story You Tell Yourself
objectives: Combine escalation of commitment, the planning fallacy about cooperation, self-serving attribution and the illusion of control into reading your own account of a situation sceptically.
Describe a real decision completely, using everything covered across both bias modules.
teach: Last week's biases distorted numbers before a decision; this week's distort the STORY told about a decision — why we're still going, why others will surely cooperate, why we won or lost, and how much control we actually had.

Assuming a story feels true because it's the one you'd naturally tell. All four of this week's biases produce stories that feel completely reasonable from the inside — that's exactly what makes them hard to catch without a deliberate check.

This closes out both bias modules. The actual skill across all eight isn't eliminating bias entirely — it's building the habit of pausing on a significant decision to check for it, using a specific, repeatable question for each one.
lessons.example: A founder keeps funding a failing product (escalation), assuming a partner will deliver an integration on time despite past delays (planning fallacy), crediting her own insight for the product's early traction while blaming the market for its later decline (self-serving attribution), and feeling that working longer hours will fix a problem that's actually about market fit, not effort (illusion of control) — four different distortions, all supporting the same comfortable story.
practicePrompts: Think of a real decision or situation you're currently telling yourself a story about.
Check it against all four: are you escalating, assuming smooth cooperation, attributing self-servingly, or overestimating your control?
Consider what an outsider, with no stake in the story, would say instead.
lessons.apply: Pick one real, current decision where you suspect your own story about it might not be fully accurate, and check it explicitly against all four of this week's biases.
lessons.reflect: In your own words, describe a real decision you're facing or recently made, and check it against as many of this module's eight biases as actually apply.

lessons.title: Reciprocity, Consistency, and Social Proof
objectives: Name three honest influence principles — reciprocity, consistency, and social proof — and use them transparently rather than manipulatively.
teach: Three well-documented influence principles: reciprocity (people tend to return a favour), consistency (people tend to act in line with commitments they've already made), and social proof (people look to what others similar to them are doing). Each can be used honestly, by genuinely offering something first, genuinely securing a real commitment, or genuinely pointing to real evidence of others' behaviour.

Treating any deliberate use of these principles as inherently manipulative. The difference between honest influence and manipulation isn't whether a principle is used — it's whether what's being offered, committed to, or pointed at is actually true and freely entered into.

Using them dishonestly — a fake favour with strings attached, a fabricated commitment, invented evidence of what others are doing — is manipulation. The same principles, used transparently, are just normal honest communication.
lessons.example: A colleague offers to cover your shift one week (reciprocity), genuinely with no expectation attached. The following month, when she asks for a swap, you're naturally inclined to help — not because she engineered an obligation, but because a real favour was given and a real willingness to return it followed.
practicePrompts: Think of a time someone's request felt easy to say yes to.
Consider whether reciprocity, consistency, or social proof was quietly at play.
Ask whether it was used honestly — was what was offered or pointed to actually real?
lessons.apply: Next time you're asking someone for something, consider honestly offering something first, referencing a real prior commitment, or pointing to real evidence of what others have done — rather than just asking cold.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you felt manipulated by one of these principles. What made it feel dishonest rather than just persuasive?

lessons.title: How You Present a Choice Shapes It
objectives: Recognise how framing a choice for someone else — not just for yourself — shapes what they pick, and use that deliberately and honestly.
teach: The same choice, offered to someone else, can be accepted or declined depending purely on how it's framed — as a gain or a loss, as the default or an opt-in, as rare or common. This isn't just something that distorts your own judgment (covered earlier); it's a real lever when you're the one presenting a choice to someone.

Presenting a choice without considering how its framing will shape the other person's decision, then being surprised by their answer. The framing is part of what you're communicating, whether you intend it to be or not.

Using framing to help someone see a choice clearly — accurately highlighting what's actually at stake — is honest communication. Using it to obscure the real choice, or push someone toward an option that doesn't serve them, crosses into manipulation.
lessons.example: Offering a colleague "a chance to lead this project" lands very differently from "extra work with no additional resources" — even if both describe the same opportunity accurately. Choosing the framing that highlights what's genuinely true and relevant to them is honest; choosing one to obscure a real downside isn't.
practicePrompts: Think of a choice you need to present to someone else soon.
Consider at least two honest ways of framing the same choice.
Pick the framing that most accurately reflects what's actually at stake for them.
lessons.apply: Next time you're presenting a choice to someone, consciously choose a framing that's both honest and clear, rather than defaulting to whatever wording comes to mind first.
lessons.reflect: Think of a choice someone presented to you that felt framed to push you a certain way. What was different about the framing versus a neutral description?

lessons.title: Saying No, Clearly
objectives: State a boundary or refusal clearly, without over-explaining it into an invitation to negotiate.
teach: A clear refusal states the boundary without extensive justification: "I can't take that on this week" is complete. It doesn't require defending, apologising for, or building an elaborate case for the no.
Padding a refusal with excessive explanation, which often invites the other person to argue with or pick apart the justification, rather than simply accepting the boundary itself.
A short reason, if one is offered at all, is fine — the problem isn't explaining, it's over-explaining to the point that the boundary itself starts to sound negotiable.
lessons.example: "I can't help with that this week, I've got too much on" is a complete, clear boundary. Adding four more sentences justifying exactly why, apologising twice, and promising to make it up somehow turns a simple no into something that reads as open for negotiation.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent request you said yes to when you wanted to say no.
Draft the clear, short version of the no you wished you'd given.
Notice how much shorter it is than the version you'd have actually said.
lessons.apply: Next time you need to decline something, give the short, clear version first, and resist the urge to pad it with extra justification.
lessons.reflect: Think of a boundary you over-explained recently. What happened as a result — did it get negotiated away?

lessons.title: What's Actually Motivating That
objectives: Look past someone's stated reason to consider other incentives that may also be shaping their position, in everyday communication.
teach: What someone says is motivating their position is real information, but it's rarely the complete picture. People have incentives — reputational, financial, social — that shape what they say and do, often without being stated or even fully conscious.

Taking a stated reason entirely at face value, missing other incentives that are also plausibly at play. This isn't about assuming bad faith — it's about recognising that stated reasons and complete motivations aren't always the same thing.

Considering a stated reason alongside what else might reasonably be in someone's interest doesn't mean distrusting everything they say — it means reading their position with the same completeness you'd want someone to read yours with.
lessons.example: A colleague says he's against a proposed office move because of the commute. That might be entirely true — and it's also worth noticing, without assuming deception, that the current office happens to be near a team he's close to, which is a separate incentive worth considering alongside the stated one.
practicePrompts: Think of a position someone recently stated to you.
Note the reason they gave.
Consider, without assuming dishonesty, what other incentive might also be in play.
lessons.apply: Next time someone states a position, note their stated reason, then separately consider what else might reasonably be motivating it, before responding.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you only learned someone's full motivation later. What would reading for other incentives earlier have told you?

lessons.title: Getting Heard, Honestly
objectives: Combine honest persuasion, framing, boundaries and reading incentives into one everyday communication.
teach: This week covered four everyday communication tools: using honest influence principles, framing a choice accurately for someone else, stating a boundary clearly, and reading the incentives behind someone's stated position.

Using only one of these in isolation — framing a request well but padding a refusal elsewhere in the same conversation, or reading someone's incentives carefully while ignoring your own framing of what you're asking for.

All four share one thread: honest, clear communication that doesn't rely on obscuring anything — not what you're offering, not what you're declining, not what you understand about the other person's position.
lessons.example: Asking a colleague for help, you reference a favour you did last month (honest reciprocity), frame the ask specifically and accurately ("an hour reviewing the draft" rather than something vaguer), and if they decline, accept a short, clear no instead of pushing — while also noting, without resentment, that they're likely also weighing their own deadline pressure (an incentive they may not have stated outright).
practicePrompts: Think of a real conversation you have coming up.
Plan how you'll frame your ask or position honestly.
Consider what boundary you might need to hold, and what incentives the other person might be weighing.
lessons.apply: Go into your next real conversation having planned all four: how you'll frame things honestly, what boundary you might need to hold, and what incentives might be shaping the other person's position.
lessons.reflect: Across this week, which of the four — honest persuasion, framing, boundaries, or reading incentives — do you most need to practise deliberately?

lessons.title: Clear and Firm, Not Aggressive or Passive
objectives: Distinguish assertive communication from both aggressive and passive communication.
teach: Assertive communication states your position, need, or boundary clearly and respectfully. It's distinct from aggressive communication (which disregards the other person's position) and passive communication (which avoids stating your own).

Equating clear, firm statements with aggression, or mistaking avoidance and over-accommodation for politeness. Both confusions lead to the same place: a real position left unstated, either out of fear of seeming aggressive, or out of habit dressed up as courtesy.
Assertiveness names what you think or need without demanding the other person agree, and without pretending you don't have a position at all — both of the other two modes skip one half of that.
lessons.example: "I disagree with this approach, and here's why" is assertive. "This approach is obviously wrong and anyone who supports it hasn't thought it through" is aggressive. Saying nothing and quietly resenting the decision later is passive. Only the first states a real position while leaving room for the other person's.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent disagreement you had, or avoided having.
Identify which of the three modes — assertive, aggressive, or passive — you used.
Draft what the assertive version would have sounded like.
lessons.apply: Next time you disagree with something, state your position clearly and specifically, without either softening it into silence or sharpening it into an attack.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you stayed passive when an assertive response would have served you better. What held you back?

lessons.title: How You Ask Shapes Whether You Get a Yes
objectives: Frame a request specifically and clearly, rather than vaguely, to make it easier to answer and more likely to succeed.
teach: A specific request — what exactly, by when, from whom — is easier to say yes to than a vague one, because it's easier to evaluate and easier to actually act on.

Making an open-ended request and expecting the other person to figure out what's actually needed. A vague ask is easy to deflect or postpone precisely because it's unclear what agreeing to it would even require.
Specificity isn't about being demanding — a specific request can still be framed as an easy, low-cost yes. It's the vagueness, not the politeness, that makes a request easy to put off indefinitely.
lessons.example: "Let me know if you can help sometime" is easy to quietly never respond to. "Could you review these three slides by Thursday morning?" is specific enough to get an actual yes or no — and, being concrete, is often easier to agree to than the vague version felt like it would be.
practicePrompts: Think of a request you've made that went unanswered or got postponed indefinitely.
Rewrite it with a specific what, by when, and from whom.
Notice how much easier the specific version would be to actually respond to.
lessons.apply: Next time you need something from someone, make the request specific — what exactly, by when — rather than open-ended.
lessons.reflect: Think of a vague request you've made that never got a real answer. What would the specific version have looked like?

lessons.title: Finding What's Valid Before Countering
objectives: Identify what's actually valid in an opposing view before responding to it, rather than countering immediately.
teach: Productive disagreement starts by identifying what's actually valid in the other view before responding to the rest. Most positions worth disagreeing with have at least one real point buried in them, even when the overall conclusion is wrong.

Countering immediately, point by point, without first acknowledging what's genuinely correct in the other side's view. This tends to make the other person defend the whole position, including the parts they might otherwise have been willing to revise.
Naming the valid part explicitly, before disagreeing with the rest, isn't a concession or a weakness — it's usually what makes the other person actually willing to hear the disagreement that follows.
lessons.example: A colleague argues against a new process, citing concerns that are mostly unfounded but including one real gap: it doesn't account for a specific edge case. Opening with "you're right that the edge case isn't covered yet" before addressing the rest makes the remaining disagreement land better than diving straight into rebuttal would have.
practicePrompts: Think of a disagreement you're currently in or recently had.
Identify one thing that's actually valid in the other person's position.
Consider how opening with that, before disagreeing, might change the conversation.
lessons.apply: Next time you disagree with someone, state what's valid in their position first, explicitly, before responding to the rest.
lessons.reflect: Think of a disagreement that went badly. Was there a valid point in the other side you skipped over on your way to countering it?

lessons.title: Knowing When Not to Speak
objectives: Use a deliberate pause or silence strategically, as a genuine choice, not a default avoidance.
teach: A deliberate pause before responding, or choosing not to say something right now, can be a genuine strategic choice — giving a heated moment time to cool, letting someone finish a thought, or simply not having anything useful to add yet.

Treating every silence, your own or someone else's, as a sign of disengagement, weakness, or avoidance. Sometimes it is — but sometimes it's the more considered response, and assuming otherwise can mean filling a pause that didn't need filling.

The useful distinction is whether the silence is a choice or a default: pausing on purpose, having decided it's the better move right now, is different from staying quiet out of habit or discomfort and calling it strategic after the fact.
lessons.example: In a tense meeting, one person pauses for a few seconds before responding to a pointed comment, rather than firing back immediately. The pause isn't avoidance — it's a deliberate choice that lets the response land more carefully than an instant reaction would have.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent conversation where you responded immediately.
Consider what a brief, deliberate pause might have changed.
Think of a time you went quiet out of habit, and ask honestly whether it was really a strategic choice.
lessons.apply: Next time a conversation gets heated or complicated, try a deliberate pause before responding, and notice what it changes.
lessons.reflect: Think of a silence — yours or someone else's — that you misread as disengagement. What was actually going on?

lessons.title: Communicating Under Pressure
objectives: Combine assertiveness, specific requests, productive disagreement and strategic timing into one difficult real conversation.
Describe a real communication challenge completely, using everything covered across both communication modules.
teach: Last week covered everyday communication tools for calm conversations; this week is the same honesty and clarity applied under pressure — disagreement, tension, a request that matters, a moment that calls for restraint.

Reaching for only one tool under pressure — staying assertive but forgetting to acknowledge what's valid in the other side, or pausing strategically but never actually stating your position once the pause is over.

This closes out both communication modules. None of the eight ideas across them require being more forceful or more accommodating by default — they're about matching your communication to what's actually true and actually needed, honestly, in each specific moment.
lessons.example: In a tense disagreement with a business partner over direction, staying assertive rather than passive or aggressive, naming what's valid in their view before disagreeing, making your actual request specific rather than vague, and pausing before responding to a pointed comment — all four at once, in one difficult conversation.
practicePrompts: Think of a real, difficult conversation you're facing or recently had.
Check it against all four: were you assertive, specific, willing to find valid points, and deliberate about timing?
Consider what you'd do differently with all four in mind.
lessons.apply: Before your next difficult conversation, plan explicitly for all four: how to stay assertive, what specific request you're making, what might be valid in the other side, and where a pause might help.
lessons.reflect: In your own words, describe a real difficult conversation you're facing or recently had, and check it against as many of this module's eight communication ideas as actually apply.

lessons.title: A Negotiation With a Bias Trap
objectives: Negotiate a real deal while recognising and correcting for a personal bias distorting your own side of it.
teach: A real negotiation rarely arrives clean. It usually comes bundled with at least one of the personal biases from weeks 8-9, quietly distorting your own reasoning before the other side ever says a word.

Treating negotiation preparation (BATNA, reservation value, ZOPA) and bias-checking (sunk cost, overconfidence, anchoring) as separate skills to apply at different times. In a real negotiation, they're checked together, on the same decision, at the same moment.

The sunk-cost and overconfidence checks from weeks 8-9 apply just as directly to a negotiation as they do to any other decision — money already spent on something you're now selling, or confidence in your own read of the market, can distort a reservation value just as easily as they distort any other number.
lessons.example: Selling a used car you've recently spent $800 repairing, you're tempted to set your reservation value higher to 'recoup' the repair cost (sunk cost), and you're '90% sure' it's worth more than comparable listings suggest, based on a gut feeling about its condition (overconfidence). A clean reservation value ignores the $800 entirely and checks your market read against actual comparable sales, not your own confidence.
practicePrompts: Think of a real negotiation you're facing or recently had.
Check your own reasoning for sunk cost or overconfidence before checking the other side's position.
Notice whether either bias has quietly shifted your reservation value.
lessons.apply: Before your next real negotiation, explicitly check your own reservation value for sunk cost and your own market read for overconfidence, before doing anything else.
lessons.reflect: Think of a past negotiation where a personal bias, not the other side's tactics, was the main thing working against you.

lessons.title: A Group Decision, Read Completely
objectives: Read a multi-party group decision completely — players, timing, information, incentives — and communicate within it assertively.
teach: A group decision with three or more people draws on the very first ideas in this course — who's actually a player, what they can choose, who knows what and when — just as much as it draws on the multi-party complications from week 7.

Treating a group decision as a simplified version of a two-party one, or treating the communication skill involved (speaking up clearly) as separate from the strategic reading of who actually has a say and what they're likely to do.

Reading the situation completely — who's a real player, what each knows, what might really be motivating each stated position — is what tells you when and how to speak up assertively, rather than guessing.
lessons.example: A five-household community group is deciding whether to fund a shared garden. Reading it completely means identifying who actually has a real say (not just who's loudest), noting that two households have already discussed it privately before the meeting (timing and information), and that one household's stated budget concern might also reflect a separate, unstated preference about garden location — before deciding how to state your own position assertively.
practicePrompts: Think of a decision involving three or more people you're part of.
Map out who the real players are, and what each might know that others don't.
Consider what's really motivating each stated position, before planning how to speak up.
lessons.apply: Before your next group decision, map out the players, timing, information, and likely incentives completely before deciding how and when to state your own position.
lessons.reflect: Think of a group decision that went differently than you expected. What would reading it completely, beforehand, have told you?

lessons.title: When the Relationship Continues
objectives: Resolve a conflict within an ongoing relationship using repeated-interaction reasoning, clear boundaries, and productive disagreement together.
teach: A conflict inside an ongoing relationship — a business partnership, a long friendship, a family arrangement — is exactly where repeated-interaction reasoning and communication skills have to work together: what you say and how you say it shapes a relationship that continues long after this one conversation.

Treating the conflict as a single, isolated negotiation, forgetting that reciprocity and the shadow of the future apply directly to how this conversation itself is conducted, not just to the arrangement being discussed.

A clear boundary and productive disagreement — naming what's valid in the other person's view before stating your own position — are what let a stable, repeated arrangement actually survive a real conflict, rather than fracturing it or papering over it.
lessons.example: A long-running business partnership hits a real disagreement over direction. Treating it with repeated-interaction reasoning means recognising that how this disagreement is handled shapes the partnership's future, not just this decision; reciprocity means engaging in good faith, matching the other partner's own good-faith effort; and stating a real boundary ("I can't agree to this direction") while acknowledging what's valid in their view is what lets the partnership actually continue past the disagreement, rather than either caving or rupturing.
practicePrompts: Think of a conflict within an ongoing relationship you're part of.
Consider how this specific conversation shapes the relationship going forward, not just the immediate issue.
Draft a boundary or position that's both clear and acknowledges what's valid in the other side.
lessons.apply: In your next conflict within an ongoing relationship, explicitly consider how the conversation itself shapes the relationship's future, and state your position clearly while naming what's valid in theirs.
lessons.reflect: Think of a relationship that was genuinely strengthened, not weakened, by how a real conflict within it was handled. What made the difference?

lessons.title: The Full Picture
objectives: Apply the full course — reading a situation, responding to a choice, dominance reasoning, repeated interaction, negotiation, personal biases, and communication — to one real, current decision.
Describe that decision completely, in your own words, as the closing synthesis of the whole course.
teach: Twelve modules back, the first lesson in this course asked a simple question: who's actually deciding, and what can they choose? Everything since — responding to a choice, dominance, repeated interaction, negotiation, your own biases, how you communicate — has been building toward reading a real, messy situation completely, and acting well inside it.

Treating this course as a set of separate topics to recall individually, rather than one integrated way of reading a situation. The actual skill was never any single idea — it was building the habit of checking a real situation against all of them, the way the last four lessons just did.

This closes the course. The real test isn't this lesson's items — it's whether, the next time a real negotiation, group decision, repeated relationship, or personal bias shows up in your own life, you actually reach for this.
lessons.example: A real decision — say, whether to continue a strained but long-standing client relationship — can be read with the whole course at once: who are the real players and what's each side's best response (module 1-2); is there a dominant strategy or a stable equilibrium here (module 3-4); what's your BATNA and the real ZOPA, if a renegotiation is needed (module 5-6); is sunk cost or overconfidence distorting your own view of it (module 8-9); and how do you communicate your actual position clearly, acknowledging what's valid in theirs (module 10-11).
practicePrompts: Pick one real, current decision in your life — not a hypothetical one.
Read it against as many of this course's modules as genuinely apply.
Notice which module's lens changes your view of the decision the most.
lessons.apply: Take the one real decision you picked, and actually use what this check revealed — don't just note it, act on it.
lessons.reflect: Across this whole course, which single idea has already changed how you handle a real situation in your daily life?

concepts.label: A player is anyone whose choice affects the outcome
An action is one of the choices a player can make
Preferences rank the outcomes for one player, from the one they like most to the one they like least
A payoff is a number for how much a player likes an outcome
Timing says who chooses when: at the same time, or one after another
Information says what each player knows when choosing, including whether they have seen the other’s choice
There is strategic dependence when your result depends on someone else’s choice as well as your own
A best response is the action that gives you the highest payoff given the other player’s choice
In a coordination situation, your best response is to match the other’s choice; in an anti-coordination situation, to differ from it
When you are unsure what the other will do, a best response to your belief is the action with the highest average payoff, weighting each of their choices by how likely you think it is
A dominant strategy gives you a higher payoff than any other action, whatever the other player does
An action is dominated when another action gives you a higher payoff whatever the other player does
Iterated elimination removes dominated actions one round at a time, then checks again in what is left
An action weakly dominates another when it is never worse and sometimes better

misconceptions.label: MODEL_EXTRA_PLAYER
misconceptions.description: Included someone who makes no choice that affects the outcome.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_MISSING_PLAYER
misconceptions.description: Left out someone whose choice affects the outcome.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_MISSING_ACTION
misconceptions.description: Left out an action a player can take.

misconceptions.label: MISREAD_PAYOFF_OWNER
misconceptions.description: Used the other player’s payoff as one’s own.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_WRONG_RANKING
misconceptions.description: Misordered a player’s preferences over outcomes.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_WRONG_INFO
misconceptions.description: Wrong account of who knows or sees what when choosing.

misconceptions.label: MODEL_WRONG_TIMING
misconceptions.description: Wrong order of choices.

misconceptions.label: IGNORED_DEPENDENCE
misconceptions.description: Treated one’s result as depending only on one’s own choice.

misconceptions.label: ACROSS_NOT_WITHIN
misconceptions.description: Compared cells across the other player’s actions instead of within one.

misconceptions.label: INCOMPLETE_COMPARISON
misconceptions.description: Compared payoffs for only one of the other player’s actions.

misconceptions.label: TREATING_TIE_AS_STRICT
misconceptions.description: Treated equal payoffs as though one action were strictly better.

misconceptions.label: NOT_BR_TO_OWN_PREDICTION
misconceptions.description: Chose an action that is not a best response to one’s own stated prediction or belief.

misconceptions.label: DOMINANCE_FROM_OUTCOME
misconceptions.description: Called an action better whatever happens because it led to a good outcome once.

misconceptions.label: IGNORED_OPPONENT_INCENTIVE
misconceptions.description: Expected the other player to pick an action that is worse for them whatever happens.

misconceptions.label: INDIVIDUAL_AS_JOINT
misconceptions.description: Assumed that choices each better for their owner give an outcome no other outcome improves on for both.

misconceptions.label: ELIMINATED_UNDOMINATED
misconceptions.description: Set aside an action that is not worse in every case.

misconceptions.label: WEAK_AS_STRICT
misconceptions.description: Called a weakly dominant action strictly dominant: treated a tie as a win when comparing across all of the other’s choices.

misconceptions.label: Equilibrium mistaken for the best outcome
misconceptions.description: Treating a stable pair of choices as the best possible result for both players, rather than simply one neither side wants to unilaterally change.

misconceptions.label: Ignored a second stable pair
misconceptions.description: Checking only one pair of choices for stability and missing that a different pair is also stable.

misconceptions.label: One-shot reasoning applied to a repeated situation
misconceptions.description: Reasoning about a choice as if this were the only round, ignoring how it will shape the other player's choices in future rounds.

misconceptions.label: Reciprocity mistaken for unconditional cooperation
misconceptions.description: Treating a reciprocal strategy as always cooperating regardless of what the other side does, rather than mirroring their last choice.

misconceptions.label: BATNA ignored
misconceptions.description: Negotiating without working out your best alternative to a deal, so there's no way to tell a good offer from a bad one.

misconceptions.label: Reservation value confused with target
misconceptions.description: Treating your walk-away point (reservation value) as the same thing as your hoped-for outcome (target), when they're different numbers serving different purposes.

misconceptions.label: ZOPA assumed without checking
misconceptions.description: Assuming a deal is possible without checking whether the two sides' acceptable ranges actually overlap.

misconceptions.label: Position mistaken for interest
misconceptions.description: Treating what someone is asking for (their position) as the same thing as what they actually want (their interest), missing room for a different solution that serves the same want.

misconceptions.label: Negotiation assumed purely distributive
misconceptions.description: Treating every negotiation as a fixed pie to be split, missing opportunities to create additional value both sides could share.

misconceptions.label: Passively letting the other side anchor
misconceptions.description: Defaulting to let the other party make the first offer without considering that doing so often shifts the eventual outcome in their favour.

misconceptions.label: Concession pattern misread
misconceptions.description: Reading a concession's size or speed as revealing something it doesn't — for instance, assuming a quick concession always signals weakness rather than a low-priority issue.

misconceptions.label: Single-issue framing
misconceptions.description: Negotiating one issue at a time instead of bundling several, missing trades that would let each side get more of what they value most.

misconceptions.label: Two-party assumption in a multi-party situation
misconceptions.description: Reasoning as if only two parties are involved when a third party's presence, alliances, or sequencing actually changes the dynamics.

misconceptions.label: Overconfidence about the other side's BATNA
misconceptions.description: Assuming you know the other party's alternatives or walk-away point without having actually verified it.

misconceptions.label: Fairness perception ignored
misconceptions.description: Focusing only on your own numeric outcome while ignoring whether the other side will see the deal as fair enough to actually accept or honour.

misconceptions.label: Walk-away point misjudged
misconceptions.description: Either accepting a deal worse than your reservation value out of momentum, or walking away from a deal that actually beat it, out of ego or overconfidence.

misconceptions.label: Overconfidence unchecked
misconceptions.description: Treating your own confidence level as evidence of accuracy, without checking it against an outside measure like a track record or base rate.

misconceptions.label: Loss aversion unrecognised
misconceptions.description: Weighing a potential loss much more heavily than an equivalent gain, in a way that distorts a decision, without recognising the asymmetry is happening.

misconceptions.label: Own estimate anchored and uncorrected
misconceptions.description: Letting an arbitrary or irrelevant first number pull your own estimate toward it, without adjusting far enough away once better information is available.

misconceptions.label: Sunk cost influencing a forward decision
misconceptions.description: Letting past, unrecoverable investment influence a decision that should only weigh future costs and benefits.

misconceptions.label: Escalation of commitment
misconceptions.description: Continuing to invest in a failing course of action to justify past investment or avoid admitting a mistake, rather than reassessing it on its current merits.

misconceptions.label: Planning fallacy about others' cooperation
misconceptions.description: Assuming other people will cooperate, respond, or deliver smoothly and on schedule, underestimating realistic friction, delay, or disagreement.

misconceptions.label: Self-serving attribution
misconceptions.description: Crediting your own skill for a win while blaming external factors such as luck or an unfair opponent for a loss, in a way that distorts what actually happened.

misconceptions.label: Illusion of control
misconceptions.description: Overestimating how much influence you actually have over an outcome that depends heavily on chance or another player's independent choice.

misconceptions.label: Ethical persuasion mistaken for manipulation
misconceptions.description: Treating any deliberate use of an influence principle as inherently manipulative, rather than recognising it can be used transparently and honestly.

misconceptions.label: Framing effect on others ignored
misconceptions.description: Presenting a choice to someone without considering how the framing itself, not just the content, will shape what they decide.

misconceptions.label: A boundary diluted by over-explaining
misconceptions.description: Padding a clear refusal with excessive justification, which invites the other person to negotiate the boundary itself rather than accept it.

misconceptions.label: Stated incentive taken at face value
misconceptions.description: Accepting someone's stated reason as their complete motivation, without considering other incentives that may also be shaping their position.

misconceptions.label: Assertiveness confused with aggression or passivity
misconceptions.description: Equating clear, firm communication with aggression, or mistaking passive avoidance for politeness.

misconceptions.label: Vague request
misconceptions.description: Making an open-ended, unspecific request that's easy for the other person to deflect or postpone, rather than a specific, answerable one.

misconceptions.label: Disagreement treated as combat
misconceptions.description: Countering an opposing view immediately without first identifying what's actually valid in it.

misconceptions.label: Strategic silence mistaken for passivity
misconceptions.description: Treating a deliberate pause or silence as always a sign of disengagement or weakness, rather than recognising it can be a considered choice.
